summary: Junior Astronaut is a browser-based pixel-art game for kids aged 7 to 12 that turns the sky over their own city into training for life on the Moon or Mars. Players choose an Earth base (Arequipa, Peru, or Tromsø, Norway), a destination and a character, then complete training missions built on real NASA data: they aim solar panels using irradiance measured by NASA POWER, take shelter from coronal mass ejections recorded in NASA DONKI, and balance water, oxygen and CO₂ like the Space Station's ECLSS. Each mission earns a tool for their backpack. Then they travel to their destination and, during a watch shift, must decide which alerts to handle first when there isn't time for all of them. No choice is free: more energy costs battery, more protection costs time. Failing is shown as a record and a lesson, not a punishment. It matters because it teaches real deep-space survival constraints starting from something familiar, the sun and weather of their own city, and it runs in the browser with no account, in four languages including Quechua.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Junior Astronaut is a narrative adventure browser game that trains children aged 7 to 12 to make astronaut-style decisions. The child chooses the Moon or Mars, picks three upgrades for their station, and then trains first on Earth, in Arequipa (Peru) or Tromso (Norway), through short mini-games that use that city's real sunlight data. Each training earns a tool for the mission. Then the child stands a five-turn watch at the outpost: two alerts arrive each turn, only one action is possible, and ignoring an alert makes it worse. Four bars (Energy, Oxygen, Protection, Food) must last until the end. Every action shows what it costs, so no choice is free: power given to the radio cannot go to the air.

HOW IT WORKS

The core mechanic is the trade-off. In the solar mini-game the child aims a panel, reads real NASA POWER sunlight values, and splits the energy between communications, the night shelter and an optional lab. Other mini-games cover air and water recycling, cabin pressure at altitude and food growing. A failed attempt explains why it failed and invites a retry; failing is shown as a record, not a punishment. A separate Station Mode lets a class or family play on one shared screen (3 to 5 children, no accounts, no servers).

REAL DATA

NASA POWER daily solar irradiance (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN) for Arequipa and Tromso, fetched from the API with a local fallback. NASA DONKI space-weather records from the May 2024 solar storm, embedded as an archived dataset and labelled as archived, not live. Every data point shows its source and status (updated, historical or fallback). The game states clearly that costs, protection levels and consequences are simulated game rules, while the data describes the Earth and the Sun.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Children feel a real constraint of deep-space survival instead of only reading facts: what you save today can cost you tomorrow. Training in their own city first gives them a familiar baseline, so the contrast with the Moon or Mars becomes meaningful. Teachers and families get a shared-screen mode with no sign-up. The game is free and plays in any browser.

TOOLS

A React web application (JavaScript) with pixel-art illustrations, hosted online and playable without download or account. Languages: English and Spanish, with Quechua and Norwegian drafts pending native-speaker review. [TEAM TO CONFIRM: other tools or libraries used.] Claude (Anthropic), a Super Intelligence (SI) tool, helped draft text and check facts against official pages; the demo narration is SI-generated synthetic voice. [TEAM TO CONFIRM: whether any illustrations or code were SI-generated.]

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It turns mission planning into a story the child lives, not a quiz. Its own twist is contextualisation: the child trains under their own sky before leaving for another world, so the learning is anchored in a place they know. Every mini-game gives a tool that matters later, so training and mission are one loop.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Plain language and short messages for ages 7 to 12; privacy by design (nicknames only, no personal data, no accounts); honesty about data (archived versus live, real versus simulated); scientific validity (each fact linked to an official source); failure without punishment; and replayability through two destinations, two cities and varied alerts. Known limits: Station Mode is a local, single-screen mockup (no multiplayer servers yet), and two languages are still drafts.

NASA DONKI: space weather database (CMEs and geomagnetic storms)
NASA DONKI: May 2024 coronal mass ejection used in the game
NASA ECLSS: Environmental Control and Life Support Systems
NASA Veggie: Space Station plant growth system
NASA OSDR: Open Science Data Repository (astronaut health and biology)
